rationale: After reading about IV induction agents, test recall of propofol induction dose in mg/kg — a classic AS known-trap.
After reading about depolarising muscle relaxants, test understanding of suxamethonium's unique mechanism — a classic knowledge trap distinguishing depolarising from non-depolarising agents.
After the malignant hyperthermia section, test ability to identify the definitive treatment — a life-or-death clinical recall.
After the Mallampati classification content, test recall of the Mallampati scoring criteria — a key AS known-trap (Mallampati vs ASA physical status are frequently confused).
After reading about paediatric airway anatomy, test understanding of why uncuffed ETT sizing differs from adults — a clinically important distinction.
After the difficult airway prediction section, test ability to identify which combination of findings most reliably predicts a difficult airway — a core clinical reasoning skill.
After the monitoring section, test recall of which monitors constitute minimum standard monitoring during general anaesthesia — a foundational safety requirement.
After the maintenance and vital organ support section, test understanding of why total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) with propofol may be preferred over volatile agents in specific scenarios.
After the emergence and extubation section, test ability to identify when extubation is safe — a key AS4.5 clinical competency.
After patient selection content for day surgery, test understanding of ASA III as a relative (not absolute) contraindication — a nuanced and commonly misunderstood point.
After the conduct of day surgery section, test recall of PONV — the dominant failure mode of day surgery and a key known-trap topic.
After the NORA section, test ability to identify the key additional hazard of providing anaesthesia outside the operating room compared to the main theatre environment.
